title: Chat System
brief: Design a chat service for one-to-one and group messages. A message must reach the other person in well under a second if they are online, and wait safely if they are not. Messages must arrive in order, never get lost, and history must be there when you open the app.

functional: Send a message to one person or to a group.
Deliver it live if the recipient is online.
Hold it and notify the recipient if they are offline.
Load the history of a conversation, newest first.
Show sent, delivered and read receipts.
Show whether a contact is online.

nonFunctional.name: Latency
nonFunctional.target: Online delivery under 200 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Ordering
nonFunctional.target: Everyone sees a conversation in the same order

nonFunctional.name: Durability
nonFunctional.target: A message that was acknowledged is never lost

nonFunctional.name: Delivery
nonFunctional.target: At least once, with duplicates hidden from the user

estimate.note: Assumptions, not facts: peak is about 3 times the average, and a message with its metadata is a few hundred bytes. Connections, not requests, set the size of the gateway fleet.

inputs.label: Messages sent per user per day
Share of users online at peak

outputs.label: Concurrent connections
outputs.note: Each online user holds one open socket.

outputs.label: Gateways needed
outputs.note: Add headroom for a zone failing.

outputs.label: Storage per year
outputs.note: One copy. Multiply by the replication factor.

api.does: Opens a socket. The server replays what was missed since lastSeq.
Sends a message. msgId comes from the client, so a retry is safe.
Tells the server this device has received up to seq.
Pages history backward from a sequence number.
Marks messages as read and informs the sender.
Registers a phone for push notifications.

data.fields: convId, seq, msgId, senderId, text, sentAt
data.store: Wide-column store, partition key convId, sorted by seq.
data.why: History is always one conversation, newest first. One partition read, no joins, and it scales out.
Small rows. lastSeq is the counter that gives the next sequence number.
Changes constantly and is cheap to rebuild. Entries expire if a gateway dies.
Looked up by user when we need to push.

evolution.title: Poll an HTTP API
evolution.problem: Start with the simplest thing that works: the app asks one server for new messages every few seconds.
evolution.change: One message service keeps messages in memory. Clients send with a request and poll to receive.

evolution.title: WebSocket gateways
evolution.problem: With 10M users polling every 2 seconds, that is 5M requests per second, nearly all of them empty. Messages also arrive up to 2 seconds late.
evolution.change: Clients keep one open WebSocket to a gateway. The gateway pushes messages the moment they exist. The load balancer only picks a gateway once, at connect time.
evolution.numbers: 5M empty polls per second become 0 requests

evolution.title: A durable message store
evolution.problem: A restart loses every message in memory, and there is no history to load.
evolution.change: The message service gives each message a per-conversation sequence number and writes it to a store partitioned by conversation id before it acknowledges. Partitioning by conversation keeps history one read away.

evolution.title: Many gateways and a registry
evolution.problem: One gateway holds about 100K sockets. Ten million online users need 100 gateways, and the sender and recipient are on different ones.
evolution.change: Every gateway records which users it holds in a connection registry, with a short expiry. The message service looks the recipient up to find their gateway.
evolution.numbers: the estimator shows how many gateways

evolution.title: Route through pub-sub
evolution.problem: The message service should not know every gateway address or keep thousands of connections open to them.
evolution.change: Each gateway subscribes to its own topic on a pub-sub bus. The message service publishes to the topic the registry names, and that gateway forwards the message down the socket.

evolution.title: Offline delivery and push
evolution.problem: About 90% of users are offline at any moment. They need the message, and a nudge to open the app.
evolution.change: If the registry has no entry, the message stays in the store and the push service sends a notification through the phone provider. On reconnect the client asks for everything after its last sequence number.

evolution.title: Presence off the hot path
evolution.problem: Showing online status means a heartbeat from every socket. At millions of sockets that would swamp the message path.
evolution.change: Gateways batch heartbeats into a separate presence service. Messages never wait for it, and status is allowed to be a few seconds stale.

steps.say: The sender's app writes the message to its open socket, with a message id it made itself.
The socket is already pinned to a gateway, so the traffic arrives at Gateway A.
The gateway hands it to the message service. That service takes the next sequence number for this conversation.
It writes the message to the store, keyed by conversation and sequence. A repeated message id is ignored. Only now is the sender told 'sent'.
It asks the registry which gateway holds the recipient. The answer is Gateway B.
It publishes the message to Gateway B's topic on the bus.
The bus delivers it to Gateway B.
Gateway B writes it to the recipient's socket.
The recipient's app acknowledges the sequence number. The service records 'delivered' and tells the sender.
The message reaches the message service the same way as before.
It is stored first. From this point the message cannot be lost.
The registry has no entry for the recipient, or the entry expired. They are offline.
The message service hands the push service a short alert, not the full text.
The push service sends it to the phone provider, which wakes the phone.
The user opens the app. It connects and says 'my last seen sequence is 41'.
The message service reads sequences 42 and up from the store.
It sends them down the socket. The app acknowledges the highest one, and the sender sees 'delivered'.

deepDives.title: Polling, long polling or WebSocket
deepDives.question: How does a message get from the server to a phone quickly?

options.name: Short polling
options.pros: Plain HTTP. Works through every proxy and is easy to build.
options.cons: Most requests return nothing. Delay is up to the poll interval. Costly at scale.

options.name: Long polling
options.pros: Still plain HTTP, and near-instant delivery. Few empty replies.
options.cons: Each message costs a new request and a reconnect. Headers are repeated. Servers still hold a request per user.

options.name: WebSocket
options.pros: One connection, both directions, tiny frames. Server can push at any time.
options.cons: Stateful: a gateway holds the user. Needs heartbeats, reconnect logic and a registry.

deepDives.pick: WebSocket, with long polling as a fallback
deepDives.because: Chat is two-way and frequent, so one open connection is the cheapest. The cost is state, which the registry and reconnect-with-resume handle.

deepDives.title: Ordering and ids
deepDives.question: How do we make every device show the same order, and make retries safe?

options.name: Wall-clock timestamps
options.cons: Device clocks drift and servers disagree by milliseconds. Two messages can tie or swap.

options.name: One global counter
options.cons: A single bottleneck and failure point, and nobody needs order between unrelated chats.

options.name: Per-conversation sequence plus a client msgId
options.pros: Order only where it matters. The counter lives with the conversation's partition. msgId makes writes idempotent.
options.cons: Needs one writer per conversation at a time. Order across conversations is undefined.

deepDives.because: Users only care that one conversation is in order. A counter per conversation scales with partitions. Time-sortable ids can still be used as the msgId, but the sequence decides the order.

deepDives.title: Where messages live
deepDives.question: Which store holds billions of messages, and how is history paged?

options.name: Relational database
options.cons: One table of trillions of rows. Sharding by hand is painful, and hot chats bring hot rows.

options.name: Wide-column or log-structured store
options.pros: Partition by conversation, sorted by sequence. Appends are cheap and a page of history is one range read.
options.cons: Few joins and weak ad hoc queries. Need to design around the access pattern.

deepDives.pick: Wide-column store, partition key convId, sort key seq
deepDives.because: Every query is 'the last 50 in this conversation' or 'everything after seq N'. Both are range reads. Page with a cursor: pass the oldest seq you have and ask for the 50 before it. Offsets drift when new messages arrive.

deepDives.title: Group fan-out
deepDives.question: When someone posts to a group, who does the work?

options.name: Fan out on send
options.pros: Each online member gets a push right away.
options.cons: A 100K-member channel means 100K deliveries per message.

options.name: Members pull from the log
options.pros: One write. Members read the conversation when they open it.
options.cons: Nothing is pushed live, so it feels slow without a nudge.

deepDives.pick: Fan out for small groups, pull for big channels
deepDives.because: Cap fan-out, say at a few hundred members. Above that, store once, tell online members 'new messages in convId' and let them fetch.

failures.impact: Every socket it held drops, maybe 100K users, and they all reconnect at once.
failures.fix: Clients reconnect with jittered backoff and send lastSeq, and the new gateway replays what was missed. Registry entries expire by TTL. Limit connect rate per gateway.

failures.impact: A message is published to a gateway that no longer holds the user, so it goes nowhere.
failures.fix: Never treat the registry as truth for delivery. The store has the message anyway, so the user catches up on reconnect. Refresh entries with heartbeats and a short TTL.

failures.impact: A retry or a lost ack makes the same message arrive twice.
failures.fix: Delivery is at least once by design. The client msgId makes the write idempotent, and the app drops any msgId it has already shown.

failures.impact: A phone on a bad network lets its socket buffer fill, and the gateway's memory grows.
failures.fix: Bound each socket's send buffer. When it is full, stop pushing, drop to offline mode and close the socket. The client catches up by sequence.

failures.impact: A huge busy conversation overloads one partition.
failures.fix: Bucket a conversation's partition by time, for example convId plus month. Cache the latest page. Rate limit senders.

scaling.limit: Gateways are limited by memory and file descriptors per machine
scaling.lever: Tune per-connection memory, then add more gateways. The registry and bus are the only shared parts.

scaling.limit: The registry holds every online user
scaling.lever: Shard it by user id with consistent hashing. Entries are small, so 10M users fit in a few GB.
Run gateway clusters per region. Route cross-region messages over the bus, and keep each conversation's writer in one home region.

recap.key: Keep long-lived sockets on a gateway fleet, store every message by conversation with a sequence number, and treat delivery as at-least-once with idempotent writes.
recap.numbers: About 50K messages per second on average and 150K at peak for 100M daily users. Around 10M sockets, so 100 gateways at 100K each. Hundreds of TB per year.
moves: Order per conversation by sequence number, never by clock
Find the recipient via the registry and route over pub-sub
Store first, then push or deliver, and resume from the last seen sequence
